rationales: +2 is not the oxidation number of chromium in dichromate.
Chromium is +6: the two chromium atoms balance the −2 charge of the seven oxygens and +2 charge of the potassium atoms.
+7 is not consistent with the neutral compound’s total charge.
+5 is not consistent with the neutral compound’s total charge.
Oxidation is the loss of electrons.
Reduction is the gain of electrons.
Hydration is the combination of a substance with water.
Hydrogenation is the addition of hydrogen to a substance.
Silver is ductile, but the textbook example of a metal drawn into an exceptionally long wire is gold.
Gold is so ductile that one gram can be drawn into a wire about one and a half kilometres long.
Iron is not the metal associated with this example of extreme ductility.
Calcium is not the metal associated with this example of extreme ductility.
Carbon monoxide is present only in small amounts in the atmosphere.
Oxygen is abundant but is less abundant than nitrogen.
Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere, the largest share.
Argon is present in much smaller amounts than nitrogen.
The O shell has eight subshells, not three.
The N shell has four subshells, not three.
The L shell has two subshells, not three.
The M shell has three subshells: s, p, and d.
The second period contains eight elements.
Eighteen elements occur in the fourth and fifth periods, not the second.
Twenty-three is not the number of elements in the second period.
Thirty-two elements occur in some longer periods, not the second.
The octet rule is not simply a description of eight electrons.
A picture of an electronic configuration is not the rule itself.
A pattern of electronic configuration is too vague to define the octet rule.
The octet rule describes atoms attaining eight electrons in their outer shell.
Eight electrons would correspond to four shared pairs, not a triple bond.
A triple covalent bond consists of three shared pairs, or six electrons.
Four electrons make two shared pairs, corresponding to a double bond.
Three electrons cannot form the three shared pairs of a triple bond.
KCl solubility changes more with temperature than NaCl’s does.
KNO₃ solubility increases markedly with temperature.
NaNO₃ solubility also changes substantially with temperature.
NaCl has only a small change in solubility with temperature.
Blockage of a light beam is not the cause of the Tyndall effect.
The Tyndall effect does not result from light passing without scattering.
The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by dispersed particles.
Passage through a beam of light does not describe the Tyndall effect.
Graphite is soft and slippery, rather than extremely hard.
Phosphorus is not extremely hard.
Diamond is extremely hard because of its strong covalent network.
Iodine is a relatively soft, brittle solid.
Copper can corrode, but its corrosion is not the common textbook example.
Rusting of iron is the common example of corrosion.
Aluminium forms a protective oxide layer, so its corrosion is less apparent.
Tin can corrode, but it is not the usual common example.
A true solution’s particles are too small to scatter light visibly.
A suspension scatters light, but the Tyndall effect is characteristically used to identify colloids.
Colloidal particles scatter light and show the Tyndall effect.
A solid mixture is not generally identified by the Tyndall effect.
A 2 M solution has the greatest solute concentration among these choices.
A 1 M solution is more concentrated than the 0.5 M and 0.25 M solutions.
A 0.5 M solution is more concentrated than the 0.25 M solution.
A 0.25 M solution is the most dilute and therefore contains the greatest proportion of water for the same solution volume.
Hydrogen has the lowest molar mass of these gases and diffuses most rapidly.
Helium is light, but its molar mass is greater than hydrogen’s.
Chlorine is much heavier and therefore diffuses more slowly.
Fluorine is heavier than hydrogen and diffuses more slowly.
